title: Subarrays With Enough Matching Pairs
statement:
You get an integer array nums and an integer k. Inside a subarray, a matching pair is two different positions i < j holding the same value.

Return how many non-empty contiguous subarrays contain at least k matching pairs.

examples.why: Three equal values form 3 pairs, four form 6. The two subarrays of length 3 and the whole array qualify; length 2 has only 1 pair.
Pairs of different values add up: [1, 2, 1, 2] has one pair of 1s and one pair of 2s. The two length-4 subarrays and the whole array qualify.
A subarray needs both 5s: start at index 0 and end at index 2 or 3.

hints: If a subarray has at least k pairs, what about a longer subarray that contains it?
Adding elements never removes pairs, so for each right end the qualifying starts form a prefix 0 … left − 1. Find the boundary with a sliding window.

Adding x to the window creates count[x] new pairs; removing x destroys count[x] − 1 after decrementing. For each right end, shrink from the left while the window still has at least k pairs, then add left to the answer.

explain.intuition:
The key property is monotonic: growing a subarray can only add pairs. So if [s, r] qualifies, every [s', r] with s' < s qualifies too. For a fixed right end, the good starts are exactly 0 … left − 1 for some boundary left, and that boundary only moves right as r grows. Classic sliding window.

Counting pairs incrementally is the second trick. When a value x enters a window that already holds c copies of it, it forms c new pairs, one with each copy. When it leaves, it takes away the pairs it had with the remaining c − 1 copies. Recounting from scratch would cost O(n) per step.
steps: Keep a map count, a running pairs total, a left pointer and the answer.
For each right end r: add count[nums[r]] to pairs, then increase that count.
While pairs ≥ k: decrease count[nums[left]], subtract the new count from pairs, and move left right.
Now every start before left works for this right end, so add left to the answer.
pitfalls: Counting distinct duplicated values instead of pairs. Three equal values make 3 pairs, not 1.
Adding n − r instead of left, or mixing up which side of the window is the free one.
Using a 32-bit counter. The answer can reach about n²/2 = 5 · 10⁹.

solutions.title: Every start, extend right
solutions.idea: Fix the start, extend the end one element at a time while updating the pair count. Once it reaches k, every longer end works too.

solutions.title: Sliding window with a pair counter
solutions.idea: For each right end, push left as far as the window still has k pairs. Every start before left qualifies.
solutions.py:
class Solution:
    def countRichSubarrays(self, nums: List[int], k: int) -> int:
        count = defaultdict(int)
        pairs = left = total = 0
        for x in nums:
            pairs += count[x]
            count[x] += 1
            while pairs >= k:
                y = nums[left]
                count[y] -= 1
                pairs -= count[y]
                left += 1
            total += left
        return total
